extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and writers seeking an overview of Māori culture and practices
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic overview of Māori cultural practices, material culture, performance, protocols, and social institutions useful as background for research or creative work. Covers motifs, weaving and clothing techniques, marae protocols, performance (kapa haka, haka), food/agriculture, waka, and funeral and oral traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marae protocols (tikanga/kawa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail of marae protocols, called 'tikanga' or 'kawa', vary by iwi but in all cases locals and visitors have to respect certain rules especially during the rituals of encounter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a group of people come to stay on a marae they are considered manuhiri (guests) while the hosts are tangata whenua ('people of the land'). The marae generally consists of an open cleared area in front of a carved meeting house (wharenui), a dining hall and other facilities. Functions include meetings, celebrations, weddings, christenings, reunions and tangihanga (funerals). Respecting local kawa is required during these rituals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pōwhiri (welcoming ceremony) structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A meeting on a marae often begins with a pōwhiri (a welcoming ceremony). The pōwhiri is structured and starts with the visitors waiting at the gate or entrance and forming group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It includes speeches following a traditional format, their sequence dictated by the kawa of that place, and is followed by waiata (songs). It is appreciated if guests can say a few words in Māori and sing a song they are familiar with as a group. Sharing of food and communal preparation (for example, a traditional hāngī) are important parts of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory expectations and oral tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Oratory is especially important in the rituals of encounter; speakers are expected to include allusions to traditional narrative and to a complex system of proverbial sayings (whakataukī).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral traditions include narratives, songs, calls, chants, haka and formalised speech patterns that recall the history of the people. Effective speech on a marae typically references tribal history and uses established proverbial material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangihanga (funeral) protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Tangihanga or tangi are the means by which the dead are farewelled and surviving family members supported; they hold central place in marae custom and take precedence over other gatherings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangihanga almost always takes place on the home marae of the deceased. It is normal for Māori to travel long distances to attend. The whānau of the deceased sit by the coffin on the porch or in the wharenui; a tangi may go on for several days, especially for a person of great mana.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kapa haka performance and competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Kapa haka (haka groups) practice and perform cultural items such as waiata (songs), action songs, haka and poi; groups are organized and often participate in national competitions where groups are judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performances may include poi dances, traditional instruments and modern instruments (guitar). National kapa haka competitions are judged to find the best performers; repertoire, precision, cultural correctness and presentation are implied performance dimensions though specific judging criteria are not listed on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Haka form and social role
rubrics_metrics.description: The haka is an action chant with hand gestures and foot stomping, originally performed by warriors before battle to proclaim strength and prowess; it is now also used by representatives (notably rugby teams) before games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are many different haka; 'Ka mate' by Te Rauparaha is one of the most widely known. The haka combines chant, gesture and movement to convey intention and challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaving (raranga) and clothing production techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Textiles were made from plants including harakeke (New Zealand flax), wharariki, tī kōuka, tōī, pīngao, kiekie and toetoe; the basis of most clothing was muka (prepared flax fibre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Muka was stripped from leaves using a mussel shell, softened by soaking and pounding with patu muka (stone pestles), and spun by rolling the thread against the leg. Colours for dyeing muka were sourced from indigenous materials. The whatu (weaving) process used warp threads twined downward by hand from a strong thread held taut between two or four upright turuturu (weaving sticks) rather than a loom and shuttle. The tāniko technique produces intricate geometric designs in many colours for belts and cloak borders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials and social meanings of traditional garments
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional garments served protection and denoted social status: two main types were a knee-length kilt/grass skirt and a rectangular cape or cloak worn over the shoulders; korowai (cloaks) in particular were symbols of high rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kahu kurī (dog-skin cloaks) were rare and highly prized. Little of the human body had to be concealed in traditional contexts; specific garments (e.g., pari/tāniko bodices) became standard costume in some performances only in the 20th century. European contact changed clothing practices and perceptions of modesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Koru motif symbolism and use
rubrics_metrics.description: The koru is a spiral shape resembling a new unfurling silver fern frond and is an integral symbol used in whakairo, tā moko and painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The koru symbolizes new life, growth, strength and peace; its shape 'conveys the idea of perpetual movement' while the inner coil 'suggests returning to the point of origin'. It is the integral motif of kōwhaiwhai designs and is used in modern branding (e.g., the Air New Zealand logo based on a Ngaru kōwhaiwhai pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wharenui / meeting house composition and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: A marae generally consists of an open cleared area in front of a large carved meeting house (wharenui), along with a dining hall and other facilities; meetinghouses became places for tribal celebrations and political meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meeting houses commonly display outside carvings and intricate interior carvings and woven panels depicting tribal history. They served to display largesse, enhance mana through feasts and entertainment, and became focal points for hapū and iwi pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waka construction and purpose-based design
rubrics_metrics.description: Waka (canoes) are built in a variety of sizes depending on their purpose, including deep-sea fishing, river crossings, war and migration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waka taua (war vessels) are large sea-going craft carrying many paddlers (historically up to 80 and lengths up to ~40 metres). Waka design choices (size, seaworthiness) are determined by intended use such as long-range travel or warfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kūmara cultivation, storage techniques and tapu protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Many special techniques had been devised to grow and especially to store kūmara so it did not rot; careful storage and the use of tapu were essential to prevent unauthorised use. Seed kūmara in particular were highly tapu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices included creating man-made soils, placing humus-rich soil near the surface, selecting north-facing slopes in some regions, and using techniques (such as ring-burning vegetation) to control caterpillars. Introduced plants and changing agricultural practices affected Māori cultivation over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child-rearing practice: whāngai (adoption/fostering)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of whāngai (adopting or fostering children) has been and still is important within Māori whānau; whāngai are adopted children raised with a whānau, most often as another member of that whānau like a brother or sister.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whāngai reflects traditional kinship and caregiving arrangements and continues to have cultural significance; it informs family structure and obligations.
